# Limits, open questions, and directions {#sec-limits}

The program's headline result, that MeshTransformer2 (MT2) is several times
more accurate than GeoTransolver and Transolver when trained on a few dozen
high-lift cases and no worse at full data, is established on one dataset over
a 36-fold range of training-set sizes, and the ingredient that carries it is
not identified. This chapter states the boundary of each claim as a fact
about the evidence, lists the open questions with the preregistered outcome
that settles each, and names what would change the recommendation.

## What is established {#sec-established}

Four things are settled to the standard of the fair-comparison protocol
(@sec-protocol). MT2 is more data-efficient than GeoTransolver and
Transolver on HiLiftAeroML surface pressure; the advantage survives every
learning-rate and training-length control, holds case by case, at every
angle of attack and on never-seen geometries, and carries through to lift
and drag coefficients (@sec-data-efficiency, @fig-hilift-data-efficiency).
At full data the two architectures are at parity on HiLift and within a few
percent on DrivAerML (@sec-full-data). MT2's contracts are verified: exact
rotation and translation covariance (@sec-pose) and, with the similarity
gauge on, insensitivity to biased sampling density (@sec-robustness-density);
MT2 also tolerates a ten-fold learning-rate change that destabilizes
GeoTransolver and trains in less peak memory (@sec-mt2-cost). On the
interior, GeoTransolver's interacting query tokens lead MT2's passive decode
(@sec-interior). And across a flow-regime boundary nothing tested
generalizes (@sec-regime-extrapolation).

## Limits of each headline claim {#sec-review-honesty}

### Data efficiency: one dataset, 35 to 1,260 cases {#sec-limits-data-efficiency}

**The data-efficiency result is a statement about 35 to 1,260 training cases
on HiLiftAeroML, not a scaling law, and the measured curve shapes are what
an adversarial reader will point at.** The quantity throughout is the
relative L2 error of surface pressure, ‖p̂ − p‖/‖p − p_∞‖ over the 10,000
sampled points of a case, averaged over the 180 validation cases shared by
every rung of the nested splits (@sec-problem, @sec-metrics). The log-log
slope of a segment is −Δ log(error)/Δ log(cases) between adjacent rungs; a
larger slope means error falls faster with data. GeoTransolver's slope is
0.50 from 35 to 210 cases and 0.74 from 210 to 1,260; MT2's is 0.43 and
then 0.25. GeoTransolver steepens as data grows and MT2 flattens. Extending
the last segment of each curve as a power law to 5,000 cases gives about
0.015 for GeoTransolver and 0.029 for MT2: a naive extrapolation puts
GeoTransolver ahead by a factor of two.

```{python}
#| label: fig-slope-extrapolation
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The slope objection, drawn. Pressure relative L2 error on the shared
#|   180-case HiLiftAeroML validation set versus number of training cases,
#|   log-log, seed means (small dots are the two seeds) for GeoTransolver
#|   (red) and MeshTransformer2 (blue); the Transolver control at its better
#|   learning rate (grey, dashed) is shown at the two rungs it was run on.
#|   Each solid segment is labelled with its log-log slope. The dotted lines
#|   extend the last measured segment of each curve as a power law to 5,000
#|   cases; they are the naive extrapolation, not a prediction, and the grey
#|   band marks the region with no measurements. How to read this: the
#|   figure shows that the two measured curves have different curvature; it
#|   does not show where either curve goes, because the shared-floor evidence
#|   (text) says the flattening may belong to the protocol rather than to
#|   MT2. Protocol: learning rate 1e-3 for GeoTransolver and MT2, 3e-3 for
#|   Transolver, 500 epochs, bf16, no augmentation, 10,000 sampled points per
#|   case, two seeds. Data: results/hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json
#|   and results/t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json.
#| code-fold: true
import json, math, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

lad = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "hilift_ladder_reduction_2026-09-03.json"))
t1 = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "t1_transolver_control_reduction_2026-09-05.json"))
rungs = [(35, "lad_hl_{a}_super_scarce_seed{s}"), (210, "lad_hl_{a}_scarce_seed{s}"), (1260, "{a}_hl_lr1_seed{s}")]
curves = {}
for arch in ("gt", "mt2"):
    xs, means, pts = [], [], []
    for n, pat in rungs:
        v = [lad[pat.format(a=arch, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
        xs.append(n); means.append(statistics.mean(v)); pts.append(v)
    curves[arch] = (xs, means, pts)
# Transolver at its better learning rate per rung (3e-3 at both rungs run).
txs, tmeans, tpts = [], [], []
for n, pat in [(35, "t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}"), (210, "t1_hl_transolver_scarce_{lr}_seed{s}")]:
    best = min(([t1[pat.format(lr=lr, s=s)]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)] for lr in ("lr1e3", "lr3e3")),
               key=statistics.mean)
    txs.append(n); tmeans.append(statistics.mean(best)); tpts.append(best)

X_EXTRAP = 5000
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 5.0))
ax.axvspan(1260, 8000, color=GRID, alpha=0.35, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(1260 * 1.06, 0.5, "no measurements", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5, va="top")
ax.plot(txs, tmeans, color=INK2, ls="--", lw=1.4, marker="^", ms=6, zorder=3)
for x, v in zip(txs, tpts):
    ax.scatter([x] * 2, v, color=INK2, s=12, zorder=4)
# Transolver label to the right of its 210-case point (clear of both solid curves)
ax.annotate("Transolver", (txs[1], tmeans[1]), xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            color=INK2, fontsize=9.5, ha="left", va="center")
style = {"gt": (RED, "GeoTransolver", "o"), "mt2": (BLUE, "MeshTransformer2", "s")}
for arch, (xs, means, pts) in curves.items():
    c, name, mk = style[arch]
    up = arch == "gt"  # GeoTransolver slope labels above its curve, MT2 below
    ax.plot(xs, means, color=c, lw=2.2, marker=mk, ms=7, zorder=3)
    for x, v in zip(xs, pts):
        ax.scatter([x] * 2, v, color=c, s=14, zorder=4)
    for i in range(2):  # slope label per measured segment
        slope = -math.log(means[i + 1] / means[i]) / math.log(xs[i + 1] / xs[i])
        xm, ym = math.sqrt(xs[i] * xs[i + 1]), math.sqrt(means[i] * means[i + 1])
        ax.annotate(f"slope {slope:.2f}", (xm, ym), xytext=(0, 9 if up else -11),
                    textcoords="offset points", color=c, fontsize=9, ha="center",
                    va="bottom" if up else "top",
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    # naive power-law extrapolation of the last measured segment
    s_last = -math.log(means[2] / means[1]) / math.log(xs[2] / xs[1])
    y_ext = means[2] * (X_EXTRAP / xs[2]) ** (-s_last)
    ax.plot([xs[2], X_EXTRAP], [means[2], y_ext], color=c, ls=":", lw=1.6, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([X_EXTRAP], [y_ext], color=c, s=28, facecolors="white", zorder=4)
    # MT2 (upper endpoint) labelled above its point, GeoTransolver (lower) below
    ax.annotate(f"{name}\nnaive extrapolation {y_ext:.3f}", (X_EXTRAP, y_ext),
                xytext=(8, -6) if up else (8, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=c,
                fontsize=9, ha="left", va="top" if up else "bottom")
    # architecture names: GeoTransolver above its 35-case point, MT2 below-left of its 210-case point
    if up:
        ax.annotate(name, (xs[0], means[0]), xytext=(0, 12), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=c, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="bottom")
    else:
        ax.annotate(name, (xs[1], means[1]), xytext=(-8, -6), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=c, fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", ha="right", va="top")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xticks([35, 210, 1260, 5000]); ax.set_xticklabels(["35", "210", "1,260", "5,000"])
ax.set_yticks([0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4]); ax.set_yticklabels(["0.01", "0.02", "0.04", "0.10", "0.20", "0.40"])
ax.set_xlim(14, 8000); ax.set_ylim(0.009, 0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Training cases [count]  (HiLiftAeroML nested splits)", color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("Pressure error\nrel-L2 [–]", color=INK2, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", labelpad=28)
ax.set_title("Measured segment slopes and the naive power-law extrapolation\n(shared 180-case validation set)",
             color=INK, loc="left", fontsize=11, pad=10)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=GRID); ax.grid(False, which="minor")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three facts bound the extrapolation. The claim is scoped to the range in
which every production CFD dataset in this program lives; no scaling-law
statement is made. The flattening may be a floor of the protocol rather than
a property of MT2: at 1,260 cases the two architectures share 70% of their
residual on identical points, the correlation between two-seed disagreement
and per-case error collapses for both, and accuracy still rises with points
per case (6,500 → 10,000 points is worth 8% for MT2), which is what a
resolution or label floor looks like (@sec-shared-floor); if both curves
approach one floor, GeoTransolver's steep segment cannot continue either.
And the shape is what a bias–variance argument predicts for a model with
more built-in prior: it starts lower and has less left to learn. None of
this is a proof; the token-count test, the third seed and the dedicated
unseen-geometry splits in @sec-open-questions are what would settle it.

### The mechanism is not identified {#sec-limits-mechanism}

**Five single-factor ablations of MT2 at 35 cases moved its error by at
most 16%, while its gap to the Transolver family is 190%; the ingredient
that carries the data efficiency is unknown** (@sec-mechanism). Adding raw
coordinates (which breaks the SE(3) contract), replacing the invariant seeds
by raw vectors, turning the similarity gauge on, turning the measure weights
off, and removing the relational routing from the encoder each changed the
35-case error by between −12% and +16%. The exactness of the contract is
not load-bearing, and no single route to invariant information is.

What the ablations do not establish is that invariant information is
dispensable, because no MT2 variant tested was ever without it: the
relational invariants to each slice anchor remain in every encoder layer of
the raw-seed variant and in every decoder block of the no-relational-routing
variant. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive raw centered coordinates,
normals and the freestream vector, and must learn every drive-relative
quantity, above all the local incidence n·d, from data. On HiLift the angle
of attack spans 4° to 22°, so incidence is the leading-order case-dependent
physics; on DrivAerML the freestream is fixed, n·d is a raw input already,
and the same ladder protocol shows the two architectures tied at its
smallest rung of 14 cases (@sec-nb-g1g2-verdict). That asymmetry is the one
candidate no ablation touched, and the transplant test in
@sec-open-questions is running. The stratified evidence says where the
advantage lives, not why: the baselines' error is flat across every angle
and geometry while MT2's tracks flow difficulty, but that does not name the
coupling.

### Regime extrapolation fails for every architecture tested {#sec-limits-regime}

**Neither architecture generalizes across a flow-regime boundary, and MT2's
structure does not change that** (@sec-regime-extrapolation). The readout is
d = (pressure rel-L2 on the sealed out-of-regime test set) / (pressure rel-L2
on in-regime validation cases). Trained at angles of attack up to 12° and
tested at 14° and above, or trained pre-stall and tested post-stall, both
architectures lose about a factor of ten, and the out-of-regime errors
(0.24–0.33) are worse than MT2 reaches from 35 in-regime cases (0.138). MT2
keeps the lower absolute error; GeoTransolver has the smaller d because its
in-regime floor is higher. Coverage of the regime, not architecture, governs
this axis; whether GeoTransolver's smaller ratio comes from its
raw-coordinate inputs is open (@sec-open-questions).

### Interior accuracy trails GeoTransolver by 2.6x {#sec-limits-interior}

**On the boundary → interior task, GeoTransolver's queries-as-interacting-
tokens lead MT2's passive equivariant decode by 2.6x on interior pressure,
and the deficit grows with distance from the wall** (@sec-interior). The
setting is DrivAerML volume fields predicted from 10,000 surface tokens at
10,000 interior query points; MT2's deficit is 2.5x near the wall and
3.3–5.4x in the far bands, the signature of missing volumetric context.
Interior queries are always decoded passively; the one attempt to supply
volumetric context while keeping that passive decode, equivariant latent
tokens placed off each slice anchor along its mean normal, made the interior
decode worse by 1.43x. Two designs are named and not measured
(@sec-interior-open): a wake-aligned probe set downstream along the
freestream direction, and a request-independent canonical probe lattice that
interacts GeoTransolver-style and from which queries decode passively.

### Exact query independence costs 2.7–3.9x and is not in the reference configuration {#sec-limits-query-independence}

**MT2's surface predictions in the reference configuration depend weakly on
which other points are sampled; making them exactly independent costs
2.7–3.9x in accuracy, so every surface checkpoint behind the headline
results is the interacting configuration** (@sec-query-independence). Query
independence means the prediction at a point does not change when the other
queried points change. In the reference configuration the heads read from
the interacting encoder tokens, and swapping the companion set moves a
point's prediction by about 7% (2% for GeoTransolver at a shared 5,000-cell
prefix). The optional query-independent configuration replaces the heads
with passive read blocks; it is exactly independent in fp64 and 2.7–3.9x
less accurate on DrivAerML surface pressure, including at matched memory.
Evaluate-anywhere semantics is a contract with a measured price.

### Cross-family transfer is a data property {#sec-limits-transfer}

**No checkpoint of any architecture tested transfers zero-shot across
vehicle families; what moves cross-family error is the diversity of the
training data, not the architecture** (@sec-industrial-mt1). The similarity
gauge, which fixes the sampling-density failure, leaves zero-shot transfer
unchanged. A claim of family-portable surface physics from any of these
architectures would need a corpus in which geometry, pose, scale and regime
vary one at a time (@sec-open-questions).

### The exact-kernel line stops at separated flow {#sec-limits-exact-kernel}

**The exact-kernel MeshTransformer (MT1) buys generalization exactly where
the kernel is the operator, and separated 3D aerodynamics is not such a
problem** (@sec-linear-suites, @sec-nonlinear-suites). On controlled
families with exact labels the exact-kernel decoder generalizes across
boundary-condition frequency content where no soft-slice mechanism tested
does, and extrapolates amplitude exactly under a declared linearity
contract. On DrivAerML pressure an exact potential-flow oracle scores rel-L2
4.8 against 0.77 for predicting the case mean, because the dominant physics
is separation, which no Laplace operator carries; on the interior task MT1
is 8x behind GeoTransolver. Structure buys generalization only where it
matches the PDE.

## Open questions, and what would settle each {#sec-open-questions}

Each question has a preregistered prediction in readout units and a
falsifier (@sec-nb-w2-prereg, @sec-nb-inv-prereg, @sec-nb-lvt-verdict,
@sec-nb-g5-prereg). Unless stated, the readout is the pressure rel-L2 of
@sec-limits-data-efficiency and MT2/GT is MT2's error divided by
GeoTransolver's at the same rung (below 1 means MT2 more accurate).

- **Is the two-seed result robust?** A third seed at 35 and 210 cases for
  all three architectures. Settled if every third-seed result lands inside
  the two-seed spread widened by 1.5x; falsified if any rung mean moves by
  more than 15%.
- **Is the approach to parity smooth?** The 510-case rung between 210 and
  1,260. Prediction: GeoTransolver 0.075–0.095, MT2 0.048–0.056, MT2/GT
  about 0.6. If MT2/GT is already 0.9 or above, MT2's curve is flat from
  210 on and the slope objection stands in full.
- **Is the flattening a protocol floor?** Both architectures at 1,260 cases
  with 20,000 rather than 10,000 sampled points per case. If the floor is
  the protocol's, both improve by a similar factor (within 5 percentage
  points). If GeoTransolver improves by 10 percentage points or more than
  MT2, the floor is MT2's.
- **Does the advantage require a varying freestream direction?** MT2 versus
  GeoTransolver on 126 geometries at a single angle of attack, against a
  matched-size mixed-angle control. If the carrier is the exact
  representation of direction dependence, MT2/GT is 0.40–0.55 on the mixed
  control and 0.80 or above at the single angle; 0.60 or below at the
  single angle falsifies it.
- **Is the advantage geometry memorization?** The unseen-geometry splits at
  210 and 40 cases, whose validation geometries appear at no angle in
  training. Prediction: MT2/GT within 0.1 of the same-size rungs (about
  0.41 at 210; 0.35–0.5 at 40). MT2/GT of 0.8 or above on either rung
  re-attributes the advantage to angle interpolation on seen geometries.
- **Are the drive-relative invariants the carrier?** GeoTransolver and
  Transolver at 35 cases with n·d, r̂·d and |r|/L appended to their inputs,
  everything else frozen (reference: MT2 0.138, Transolver 0.40,
  GeoTransolver 0.39). Carrier identified if both reach 0.235 or below
  (halfway to MT2 in log-error), fully identified at 0.16 or below (within
  1.15x of MT2); falsified if both stay at 0.30 or above. A mixed outcome
  is read per architecture.
- **Does GeoTransolver's smaller regime-extrapolation ratio come from raw
  coordinates?** MT2 with a raw-coordinate channel on the stall split.
  Confirmed at d of 11.0 or below with out-of-regime pressure below 0.245;
  refuted at d of 12.0 or above or pressure of 0.255 or above.
- **Can off-surface context be supplied without giving up the passive
  interior decode?** Wake-aligned probe tokens, and a request-independent
  canonical probe set that interacts GeoTransolver-style. The bar the
  previous off-surface design failed is interior pressure within 1.5x of
  GeoTransolver's. Neither launches until the carrier question is settled,
  because its answer decides which architecture the interior work builds on.
- **Which generalization axes does structure buy, one at a time?** A 3D
  RANS corpus generated with counterfactual twin draws per factor (pose,
  scale, Reynolds number, layout, mesh), so each axis is tested exactly.
  Preregistered: on pose twins GeoTransolver without a freestream frame
  fails by 5x or more and canonicalized GeoTransolver matches MT2 within
  1.05x; on scale twins at fixed Reynolds number across 0.02–20 m (the
  first real test of the similarity gauge) GeoTransolver exceeds 2x at a 10x
  scale change; on Reynolds twins no architecture transfers a decade of Re
  better than another; mesh twins set the floor below which no difference
  is reportable. The arms are void unless twin draws are adopted at
  generation time, which is why the preregistration precedes the corpus.

## Engineering directions {#sec-future}

**Memory headroom.** MT2's relational readback was written as
project-then-pool, which saves a (points × slices × hidden/2) activation per
layer for the backward pass; because the projection is affine and the slice
mixture is a softmax, pooling first and projecting second is an exact
identity (fp64 maximum difference 4e-15) that saves a (points × 8)
activation instead. Peak training memory at 10,000 tokens fell from 9.8 GB
to 3.6 GB, below GeoTransolver's 4.6 GB, with no change in function
(@sec-mt2-cost, @sec-nb-geo-pool-memory); every trained MT2 checkpoint in
this book came from the earlier implementation. The headroom is what makes
the 20,000-token floor test and larger point budgets affordable.

**Measure weights: a training-time cost and an inference-time gain.** MT2
weights each surface point by its cell area in the slice routing and the
pooled anchors. Under uniform 10,000-point sampling the weights are a source
of gradient variance rather than information: turning them off improves the
35-case error by 12% (0.88x). Together with the similarity gauge they are
also what make MT2 insensitive to sampling density at inference: 1.20x
degradation under a 10:1 biased density against 13–14.5x for the constant
gauge and 3.6x for GeoTransolver (@sec-robustness-density). The trade has
not been measured as a trade; training without weights and evaluating under
biased density would put the cost and the gain on one table.

**Area-proportional sampling, untested.** Sampling points with probability
proportional to cell area, so that every sampled point carries equal measure
and the explicit weights become uniform, would remove the gradient-variance
cost while preserving the measure semantics of the routing. It moves density
robustness from the model to the sampler, which is acceptable in training
and a liability at inference if the query cloud is not under the model's
control. Nothing in the program has measured it.

## What would change the recommendation {#sec-review-roads}

The current recommendation is GeoTransolver where interior accuracy is the
target, and MT2 for surface prediction where training data are scarce or
exact pose or density contracts are required (@sec-interior,
@sec-data-efficiency). Three outcomes would change it.

**GeoTransolver with invariant inputs becomes the production surface
model** if the transplant test lands both baselines at 0.16 or below at 35
cases and the 510-case rung and the 20,000-token test show GeoTransolver
keeping its steeper large-data slope. The small-data advantage would then be
a portable feature, three scalars per point, and MT2's remaining case would
be its contracts, of which the canonical-frame GeoTransolver already matches
pose invariance at 1.01x cost (@sec-pose).

**MT2 becomes the surface recommendation across the whole data range** if
the transplant test stays at 0.30 or above for both baselines, the
unseen-geometry ladder holds within 0.1 of the same-size rungs, the
510-case rung lands near MT2/GT 0.6, and the token test moves both
architectures by a similar factor: the advantage is then architectural and
the flattening is the protocol's floor. The interior stays with
GeoTransolver until a probe design closes the gap.

**A hybrid becomes the single production model** if a request-independent
canonical probe set brings MT2's interior pressure within 1.5x of
GeoTransolver's while keeping its surface accuracy and contracts. Such a
hybrid, MT2's encoder and surface heads with a GeoTransolver-style
interacting core on a fixed probe lattice, would be priced against MT2's
query-independent configuration, which pays 2.7–3.9x on the surface task at
matched memory (@sec-query-independence), and against a canonicalized
GeoTransolver rather than against MT2 alone. If none of these fires, the
recommendation stands as written, with the bounds of this chapter attached.
